summary:
For the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we developed TerraScope - Mars Map, an interactive, web application designed navigate mars.

TerraScope uses real NASA Viking orbital imagery and Perseverance Mastcam-Z panoramic imagery. Terrain elevations, mineral/resource sites, environmental conditions, danger zones, and LIFELINE safety scores are synthetic demonstration data. Route planning operates on that mock dataset. 

As manned missions to Mars transition from theory into reality, precise navigation is necessary for astronaut safety and mission efficiency.
details:
TerraScope Mars Map - By Celesta

What it does

TerraScope Mars is a web-based planning tool that helps a human explorer prepare a safe, productive Marswalk in Jezero Crater, where NASA's Perseverance rover landed. It stacks several views of the same place into one interface, so a planner can move from the whole planet down to a step-by-step route without switching tools:

1. Orbital view (real NASA data): an interactive 3D Mars globe built from the NASA Viking colour mosaic (NASA/JPL/USGS, distributed by ASU). Users drag to rotate, zoom in, and fly straight into Jezero Crater.

2. Ground view (real NASA data): an explorable 360° panorama from Perseverance's Mastcam-Z camera (142 images captured on Sol 3, 21 Feb 2021; NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS/ASU). It shows what an explorer would actually see standing at the landing site.

3. LIFELINE safety layer: a 3D model of a 50 × 50 km Jezero study area (65 × 65 grid, 8,192 triangles). Every cell gets a safety margin from 0 to 100:

margin = 100 − 2·slope° − 0.32·dust index − 1.1·distance from base (km)

Terrain is coloured Favourable (≥65), Caution (40–64) or Critical (<40), so hazards are visible at a glance.

4. Route planning: the user picks a destination (habitat, science or resource sites) and TerraScope plots a route from the base using Dijkstra pathfinding weighted by safety margin. It reports distance, the minimum safety margin along the way, and whether the route crosses critical terrain. A replay animates the route.

5. Mission context: a live Mars clock (Sol, local mean solar time), a surface temperature readout, an Earth Observer that calculates the real-time distance and radio delay from the user's city on Earth to Jezero, an ISS pass predictor, and a solar-system view using JPL orbital elements.

6. Mission API: every layer is also available through a documented REST API (OpenAPI/Swagger), so other tools can query terrain, safety scores and routes.

Honest scope

The orbital and ground imagery is real NASA data. The Jezero elevation model, LIFELINE inputs, candidate sites and weather values are simulated for this prototype, and the app labels them that way on screen ("Synthetic Jezero · Simulated planning"). We chose to be transparent rather than overstate what a weekend prototype can verify.

Benefits

- One screen replaces several disconnected datasets. A planner sees where they are, what it looks like, and how dangerous it is.

- Safety becomes a single number with clear tiers, so non-specialists can make good decisions quickly.

- Routes are chosen for safety, not just shortest distance, and the tool flags when a route enters critical terrain.

- It runs in any browser with no installation, so it can be shared with a crew, a classroom or the public.

Intended impact

Before people walk on Mars, every surface excursion will need careful planning around slope, dust, distance from shelter and limited time outside. TerraScope shows how layered, multi-mission data can make that planning faster and safer. The same approach also works for education: students can stand inside a real Perseverance panorama, then plan their own expedition and see why some routes are safe and others aren't.

Tools and technologies

- Frontend: JavaScript (native ES modules, no build step), HTML5 Canvas for a custom ray-cast Mars globe and the 3D terrain renderer, CSS.

- Backend: Python 3 with Flask, SQLite for sites, routes and logs, and a REST API documented with OpenAPI 3.0 / Swagger UI.

- Algorithms: Dijkstra pathfinding with safety-weighted edges (the engine supports balanced, safest, fastest and energy-saving modes), bilinear terrain sampling, slope calculation, topocentric Earth–Mars ephemeris, and Mars time (Sol / LMST) calculation.

- Testing: pytest for the backend and the Node.js test runner for the frontend math, pathfinding and scoring thresholds.

- Deployment: GitHub and static web hosting (GitHub Pages / Vercel). No special hardware is needed.

- NASA data: Viking MDIM colour mosaic (NASA/JPL/USGS via ASU), Perseverance Mastcam-Z 360° panorama (PIA24264, NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS/ASU), JPL planetary orbital elements.

What makes it creative

- It puts a planner 'on the ground' with a real Perseverance panorama, not just above Mars looking at a map.

- LIFELINE compresses several hazards into one score with clear tiers, then uses it to drive routing, so the map doesn't just show danger, it routes around it.

- The Earth Observer connects the user's own city to Jezero with real distance and radio delay. That makes the communication lag an astronaut would face tangible.

- The interface draws labels "real imagery / clear limits" right into the experience, separating measured data from simulation.

Factors we considered

- Safety first: slope, dust exposure and distance from the habitat were chosen as the main hazards for a person on foot, with conservative tier thresholds.

- Data honesty: real data and simulated data are clearly separated and labelled, with full image credits.

- Accessibility: it runs in any modern browser, with keyboard controls for globe and panorama navigation and a readable, high-contrast interface.

- Extensibility: a clean API and modular layers make it straightforward to swap the simulated terrain for real orbital elevation data (HiRISE / CTX digital terrain models) and add more layers, such as CRISM mineral maps, THEMIS thermal data and MEDA weather records.
